items.t: Occidental Petroleum stock sets 6 billion dollar debt target after Q3 milestone
sum: Occidental Petroleum announced its third-quarter results on November 9, reporting a major debt milestone alongside production above the midpoint of guidance. The company said it reduced principal debt to 10.0 billion US dollars after retiring 10.4 billion US dollars since the beginning of 2026.

The MarketScreener reproduction of the company release said Occidental generated 4.1 billion US dollars of operating cash flow from continuing operations and 2.8 billion US dollars of free cash flow before working capital. Reported diluted earnings per share were 1.61 US dollars, while adjusted earnings per share from continuing operations reached 1.91 US dollars.

Global production averaged 1.427 million barrels of oil equivalent per day in the third quarter. Permian and Rockies operations offset a temporary curtailment at certain Gulf of America facilities caused by a third-party gas pipeline constraint and maintenance work.

Management also pointed to lower realized crude prices as a factor affecting oil and gas results. The company continues to emphasize debt reduction, operating efficiency and capital discipline while advancing its lower-carbon activities.

After reaching the 10.0 billion US dollar principal-debt milestone, Occidental has established a further target of 6.0 billion US dollars. Reaching that level would reduce the company's interest expense run rate and could support greater financial flexibility through the commodity cycle.

Occidental ожидает, что капитальные расходы на начало 2027 года составят примерно 5,9 миллиарда долларов США. items.t: Should You Pick Occidental Stock Over Its Competitors?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Over its last four quarters, Occidental Petroleum (OXY) grew revenue faster than any of five oil and gas peers. Yet its stock trades at the lowest multiple of earnings in the group. Part of that low multiple comes from a single quarter in which profit ran far ahead of what Occidental’s operations earned. So how much less are you paying for Occidental than for a rival it outgrew?

Occidental trades at 6.9 times earnings, compared with 14.0 times for fellow oil and gas producer ConocoPhillips. One quarter lifts Occidental’s earnings, however: in fiscal Q1 2026, the company booked a $3.35 billion profit on $0.927 billion of operating income.

Measured on sales and operating profit instead, Occidental is still ahead. Its revenue grew 34.7% over its last four quarters, against 13.3% at ConocoPhillips. It also kept 29.3% of its sales as operating profit, against 24.7% at ConocoPhillips, so you would be paying less for a company that grew faster and earned a wider margin. Set against operating profit instead of earnings, Occidental’s $57.0 billion market value is about 7.8 times its $7.32 billion of operating profit over those four quarters. ConocoPhillips’ $162 billion is about 9.6 times its $16.8 billion. On the same measure, EOG Resources ($78.5 billion against $10.9 billion) and Diamondback Energy ($49.9 billion against $7.4 billion) cost less than Occidental.

Among the group of six, Occidental ranks first on revenue growth and third on operating margin, trailing EOG Resources and Diamondback Energy. Yet its stock return over the past year ranks only fifth, placing it ahead of Diamondback Energy alone.

Occidental earns almost all of its revenue from oil and gas. In fiscal 2025, its oil and gas segment had $20.9 billion of revenue, against $1.28 billion for midstream and marketing. That fiscal year ended in December 2025, three months after the twelve months to September 2025.

The recovery held in the latest quarter, when revenue rose 19.0% from a year earlier. Management said its U.S. onshore wells beat the midpoint of its own production forecast, more than making up for lower output in the Gulf of America and abroad.

sum: Occidental Petroleum reported a strong third quarter on Monday, November 9, 2026, combining resilient production with a major balance-sheet milestone. The earnings release, carried by MarketScreener, said the company reduced principal debt to 10.0 billion US dollars after retiring 10.4 billion US dollars since the start of the year.
Occidental Petroleum stock traded at 51.63 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 14:09 CET on Wednesday, November 11, 2026.

Net income attributable to common stockholders reached 1.6 billion US dollars, or 1.61 US dollars per diluted share, for the quarter ended September 30. Adjusted income from continuing operations was 2.0 billion US dollars, producing adjusted diluted earnings of 1.91 US dollars per share. Occidental said the difference mainly reflected losses from derivatives.

Operating cash flow from continuing operations totaled 4.1 billion US dollars. Free cash flow before working capital, a non-GAAP measure, came to 2.8 billion US dollars after 1.3 billion US dollars of capital spending. The release cautioned that such adjusted measures are not calculated under US GAAP and may not be directly comparable with similarly named measures used by other companies.

Occidental repaid 1.8 billion US dollars of principal debt during the quarter. Management said the new target is a 6.0 billion US dollar principal-debt milestone. Reaching that level would reduce annual interest expense to approximately 400 million US dollars, according to management commentary reported after the results.

Global production averaged 1,427 thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day, exceeding the midpoint of company guidance. Stronger performance in the Permian and Rockies helped offset a temporary curtailment at certain Gulf of America facilities caused by a third-party gas pipeline constraint and maintenance work.

The upstream result came despite weaker realized crude prices. Worldwide realized crude prices fell 11% from the second quarter to 85.91 US dollars per barrel, while oil and gas pre-tax income declined to 2.6 billion US dollars from 2.8 billion US dollars. Domestic realized gas prices improved sharply, partly offsetting the pressure from crude.

Occidental Petroleum (OXY) closed up 5.88% on July 7, 2026, and the reason had almost nothing to do with the company itself. A projectile struck a Qatar-owned liquefied natural gas carrier near the Omani coast as it exited the Strait of Hormuz, the shipping chokepoint that carries a large share of the world’s seaborne crude. WTI crude jumped back above $69 a barrel, a one-week high, and the most oil-sensitive large producer in the United States jumped with it.

That is the whole case for OXY in one sentence, and it is also the problem. This is a stock that trades as a direct read on the oil price, so a geopolitical scare lifts it fast, and a supply glut drags it down just as fast. The question investors are actually asking is not whether Occidental is a good oil company. It clearly is. The question is whether $51.68 is a price worth paying for a business whose fortunes are set in a market it does not control.

The single-day pop hides how rough the last few months have been. OXY carried a max drawdown of 27.63% as of July 1, 2026, and the stock still sits well below its 52-week high of $67.45. The July 7 rally was a bounce inside that damage, not a breakout from it.

Look past the one-day headline, and the supply picture turns bearish. Even as the Hormuz strike lifted prices, crude remained near its lowest level since late February. OPEC+ approved another production increase for August, and Saudi Aramco cut its Arab Light price to Asian buyers by $11 a barrel, the kind of discount last seen during the price wars of 2020 and 2015. Hormuz vessel traffic was already normalizing. For a company this levered to realized prices, a softening oil market matters more than a single tanker headline.

Management knows the exposure and has mostly chosen to live with it. On the Q1 2026 earnings call, Chief Financial Officer Sunil Mathew explained why Occidental rarely hedges: “We have not historically been active in hedging as we believe we create shareholders over the long term by maintaining exposure to commodity prices.” That matters because it tells you what you are buying. When oil rises, OXY captures the upside in full. When oil falls, there is little cushion.

sum: As peace negotiations between the United States and Iran stall, Occidental Petroleum (OXY) saw its stock rise on Monday, along with oil prices.

According to relevant reports, the negotiations have broken down, prompting oil prices to jump by approximately 5%. Iran has stated that it will resume efforts to block shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. This critical waterway carries about 20% of the world’s crude oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) transport. Iran and its allies have also threatened to block other vital shipping channels.

Industry experts have warned that energy prices could soar if these shipping disruptions are not resolved. Neil Chapman, Senior Vice President at Exxon Mobil, believes that oil prices could reach $160 per barrel within the next few weeks as inventories are gradually depleted.

To address the shortfall in energy transport from the Middle East, governments in Europe and Asia are turning to U.S. producers for oil and LNG supplies. U.S. oil exports surged more than 30% in April compared to before the Iran conflict broke out in February, reaching 5.2 million barrels per day. As one of the largest independent oil and gas producers in the United States, Occidental Petroleum is helping to meet global demand for reliable energy supplies.

Occidental Petroleum is also acquiring a 10% interest in a large deepwater exploration block near Trinidad and Tobago from Exxon Mobil (XOM). The oil major previously held 100% interest in the Ultra Deep 1 block (referred to as UD1). Exxon Mobil originally obtained the block last year through an agreement with the government of Trinidad and Tobago.

Exxon Mobil is currently conducting seismic surveys in the area, which are expected to be completed by the end of this year. Exxon Mobil now plans to invest $42 million in seismic data collection and up to two exploration wells, with drilling possibly beginning within six months of completing the seismic studies. If the block proves to be as resource-rich as Stabroek, Exxon Mobil believes that full development could require an investment of $21.7 billion in the future. Warren Buffett’s War-Time Investing Philosophy Is Playing Out in Real Time
sum: As structural macro shifts replace short-term geopolitical headlines, Warren Buffett’s long-held philosophy on resource-backed investing is facing a real-time examination. So far, his playbook is holding up.

Buffett has argued for decades that during periods of macro uncertainty or heightened geopolitical risk, the worst move an investor can make is to retreat to cash. In a widely referenced 2014 CNBC interview that has been recirculated heavily, he stated:

“If we went into some very major war, the value of money would go down… The last thing you’d want to do is hold money during a war… You’re going to be a lot better off owning productive assets… than pieces of paper.”

His logic remains straightforward: conflicts and supply chain constraints disrupt markets, but businesses that produce real goods and services, especially in energy and essential commodities, continue generating value over time. Governments can print currency, but they cannot instantly manufacture new productive capacity or replace a multi-year supply deficit.

The clearest demonstration of this philosophy in action is Berkshire Hathaway’s acquisition of OxyChem. The $9.7 billion deal for Occidental Petroleum’s industrial chemicals business closed on January 2, 2026, when commodity prices were still near multi-year lows. WTI crude had hit a 12-month low around $55 in December 2025, just weeks earlier. Buffett’s team locked in a high-quality industrial asset at a depressed valuation, classic Oracle of Omaha timing.

While initial headlines focused on short-term spikes through the Strait of Hormuz, the broader energy market has transitioned into a structural capacity deficit. Abu Dhabi National Oil Company’s (ADNOC) multi-year supply warnings indicate that global crude constraints will likely persist well into 2027. Consequently, spot prices have broken out of their early spring lulls, with WTI crude trading up near $95.99 per barrel as structural supply undercurrents outlast temporary diplomatic headlines.
